Hitchens's claim that belief in God is consoling wishful thinking—a projection of human hopes rather than a response to reality.
McGrath grants that desire cannot make a proposition true, argues that it cannot make it false either, and suggests atheism may satisfy a wish to escape accountability.

Religious belief can be a defensible interpretation of public evidence without claiming privileged knowledge, proof, or certainty, because every worldview rests on contestable judgments of explanation.
This is the pro side's concluding defense of religious intellectual credibility, reframing faith as an open and contestable explanatory judgment rather than inaccessible special knowledge.
Hitchens's closing charge that McGrath claims knowledge of God, resurrection, miracles, and salvation that he cannot conceivably possess.

McGrath defends asking why anything exists, denies privileged access, characterizes observations as publicly interpretable, and presents Christian faith as his best explanation while acknowledging that it cannot be proved.
